sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The moving parts are four, and each has a job:

The struct carries the DATA the caller will branch on — fields are the whole point. What fields? Ask what the caller's next line will be: RetryAfter for a rate limiter, Name for a lookup miss, Status for an HTTP layer. The struct is the caller's API into the failure.

The Error() method makes it an error — Go's structural typing means no registration, no inheritance; implement the one method and you're in the club. The message should render the fields (so logs are useful even where the caller doesn't use errors.As), but the fields are for code and the message is for logs — different audiences.

The pointer receiver serves two mechanics: identity (comparing *NotFoundError values — the As target matches by pointer) and nil-ness (a *NotFoundError variable starts nil). The convention: pointer, always — the ecosystem's As targets are written pointer-style, and consistency keeps the As patterns uniform.

The constructor is ordinary but deserves the standard shape:

```go
func NewNotFound(name string) error {
    return &NotFoundError{Name: name}
}
```
Returning error (not *NotFoundError) is the standard API choice: the caller sees the interface, uses errors.As when they need the fields, and your function signature stays the honest 'I can fail with various things.'

The pattern's economy: one struct, one method, one constructor — and the failure carries machine-readable data instead of prose. When a codebase's errors need MORE (codes, HTTP statuses, retryability), the extensions are methods on the same struct — the design extends without a rewrite.

questions.question: How do callers inspect a custom error?
questions.title: Callers Inspect A Custom Error
questions.direct_answer: var target *MyError; errors.As(err, &target) — walks the wrap chain, finds the first error of that type, copies it into target.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: var target *MyError; errors.As(err, &target) — walks the wrap chain, finds the first error of that type, copies.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
errors.As is the extraction tool:

```go
var rateLimited *RateLimitError
if errors.As(err, &rateLimited) {
    time.Sleep(rateLimited.RetryAfter)
    retry()
}
```

The pattern always has the same shape: declare a target of the error's type (pointer, because methods hang on pointers), pass its address to As, and As fills it if the chain contains a match. The wrap chain is traversed the same way Is traverses it — so intermediate layers wrapping with %w don't hide your type from the caller.

The pointer-vs-value detail matters: if your Error() method has a pointer receiver, the error stored in the chain is a *NotFoundError, so the target must be *NotFoundError — var target NotFoundError with &target makes As look for a value type and never match. This mismatch (value target for a pointer error) is the most common As bug, and it compiles cleanly — it just returns false forever.

As answers 'does this failure carry typed data, and give me that data.' Is answers 'is this failure this specific sentinel.' Together they cover the two reasons a caller inspects errors at all.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
errors.As is a two-phase tool, and each phase has a failure mode worth knowing.

Phase 1 — the walk: As follows Unwrap edges (linear and []error branches) like Is. It succeeds when it finds an error assignable to the TYPE of the target pointer's pointee. The chain may hold your type once, wrapped three layers deep — As finds it through all of them.

Phase 2 — the assignment: the found error is assigned into *target — the caller's variable now holds the concrete struct with its fields, and the branch proceeds.

The failure modes:
- Pointer mismatch: error stored as *NotFoundError, target is NotFoundError (or vice versa) — no match ever, compiles clean. The fix is the ecosystem convention: always pointer on both sides.
- Multiple types in the chain: As returns the FIRST match — if two layers wrapped with different types and both match, you get the outer one. Rare, but worth knowing when debugging 'wrong field values.'
- The target must be a non-nil pointer to a type implementing error — As panics otherwise. The var pattern (`var e *MyErr; errors.As(err, &e)`) is the safe shape.

When to use As vs Is: Is when the question is identity against a KNOWN value (a sentinel, a class representative). As when the question is about DATA — you need the fields. The practical ratio in real code: Is for control flow (is this retryable/cancelled/not-found), As when the handler uses failure details (log the name, sleep the duration, render the field).

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The decision is about what the CALLER can do next — and the progression from sentinel to type is the story of every maturing codebase.

Sentinel (errors.New): the caller gets identity — a bit. 'Was it ErrNotFound?' — branch on it. What the caller CANNOT do: ask which record, what status, how long. The sentinel's message is prose; parsing prose is the forbidden path (it couples the caller to your wording).

Type (struct + Error()): the caller gets identity AND data. errors.As extracts the struct; the fields are machine-readable facts. The caller's next line uses them: sleep target.RetryAfter, render target.UserMessage, log target.Name.

The forcing function in real code: the first time a caller NEEDS a fact the message carries. A retry wrapper that needs to know the backoff duration can't branch on ErrRateLimited — it needs the duration. An HTTP error renderer that needs the status code can't parse 'bad request' — it needs the number. That moment — 'the handler needs the failure's details' — is the migration point, and it arrives predictably: retry logic, error responses, metrics with labels, partial-failure reports.

The standard library's own fossils tell the story: os.ErrPermission (sentinel — 'permission denied' is a complete answer) beside os.LinkError (type — Op, Old, New fields, because 'which link, which end?' is the first question a caller of symlink code asks). Both exist because both are right — the question decides the tool. The interview version: sentinels answer WHAT, types answer WHAT AND THE DETAILS; pick by whether the caller's next action needs the details.

questions.question: Should custom errors be pointer or value receivers?
questions.title: Should Custom Errors Be Pointer Or Value
questions.direct_answer: Pointer receivers, and errors.As with a pointer target — the ecosystem convention. Mixing value and pointer error types is the classic As-mismatch bug.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Custom Error Types Basics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Pointer receivers, and errors.As with a pointer target — the ecosystem convention.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Convention: pointer. Declare the type's Error() on the pointer, return &MyError{...}, and match with a pointer target in errors.As:

```go
func (e *NotFoundError) Error() string { ... }   // pointer receiver
return &NotFoundError{Name: name}               // pointer value

var target *NotFoundError                       // pointer target
errors.As(err, &target)
```

The receiver and the target must agree: As matches the dynamic type in the chain against the target's type. Pointer error, pointer target — match. Value error (Error() on the value receiver, stored as a value), value target — match. Mixing them is the silent bug: a pointer error against a value target compiles and always returns false, because a *NotFoundError is not assignable to NotFoundError.

Why pointer won as the convention: pointer receivers are Go's default for anything with identity semantics, they keep large error structs cheap to pass, they allow nil-ness (var x *MyError is nil before assignment), and one rule everywhere beats two rules matched by discipline. The standard library's typed errors (os.PathError, net.AddrError, etc.) are pointer-style. When in doubt, look at what the ecosystem does and do that — error code is read by strangers.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[send ch <- v] --> F{buffer free?}
    F -->|yes| B[write to ring buffer]
    F -->|no / cap 0| W[park goroutine in send queue]
    R[receive <-ch] --> F2{buffer has value?}
    F2 -->|yes| D[deliver + wake sender]
    F2 -->|no| W2[park in recv queue]
    W -->|receiver arrives| C[copy sender stack → receiver stack]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The pointer convention isn't style — it's what makes the As-matching machinery line up, and the mismatch is the classic silent bug.

The mechanics: errors.As(err, &target) walks the chain looking for an error assignable to the target's TYPE — the pointee of your pointer. A chain holding *NotFoundError (a pointer) matches a *NotFoundError target — the types agree. A value error (NotFoundError, no pointer) matches a value target. Cross them — pointer error, value target — and the assignability test fails for every node: *NotFoundError is not assignable to NotFoundError (different types), so As returns false forever. The code compiles (As takes any target), runs, and quietly never matches.

Why the ecosystem standardized on pointers:
- Methods on pointers are Go's default for anything with identity (every standard library error type: *os.LinkError, *net.AddrError, *time.ParseError — all pointers).
- The nil state: var target *NotFoundError starts nil — a clean 'not yet extracted' sentinel before As runs.
- Cheap passing: the error is one pointer wide, no matter the struct size.
- ONE convention beats two matched by discipline — every As is the same shape, and reviewers never check receiver-vs-target agreement.

The audit rule for a codebase mixing them: grep for value-receiver Error() methods — each is a latent As-mismatch for callers using the pointer idiom, or a signal the error was never meant for As. The fix is mechanical (add the star) but version-locked (value-errors in the wild change identity when converted) — which is why pointer-from-day-one is the cheaper habit.

questions.question: What is the error interface exactly?
questions.title: Rror Interface Exactly
questions.direct_answer: One method: Error() string. Everything else — wrapping, Is, As, Unwrap — is the errors package's machinery built on top.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Custom Error Types Basics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: One method: Error() string.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The interface that everything else stands on:

```go
type error interface {
    Error() string
}
```

Any type with that method IS an error — no registration, no inheritance, no base class. errors.New's *errorString, fmt.Errorf's wrappers, your structs, third-party types: all just implement Error().

The important separation: the interface itself carries nothing but the message. Wrapping (%w), matching (errors.Is), type extraction (errors.As), chain traversal (Unwrap) are all behaviors of the errors package operating on errors that choose to participate — an error implements Unwrap() to join the wrapping machinery, Is(error) bool to customize matching, and so on. A bare struct with only Error() is a fully valid error; it just can't be wrapped-into or inspected beyond its message.

That minimalism is the design: one method makes errors universal (anything can fail with anything), and the optional protocol methods (Unwrap, Is, Unwrap []error) layer on capabilities without bloating the base contract. When you understand that the interface is just Error() and the errors package is a protocol on top, the whole error system stops being magic — it's interfaces all the way down, which is Go's answer to most questions.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q[the question] --> R[the core rule]
    R --> EX[the small example]
    EX --> B[the boundary — where the rule ends]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The interface's minimalism is a design decision with consequences worth tracing:

type error interface {
    Error() string
}

ONE method means ANYTHING can be an error. A string wrapper (errors.New's *errorString), a formatted chain node (fmt.Errorf's *wrapError), your structs, a third-party HTTP error, a channel-closed sentinel — if it has Error() string, it flows through every return, every if err != nil, every errors.Is/As. No registration, no inheritance, no hierarchy to keep compatible. That's why error-returning code composes across packages that have never heard of each other.

But ONE method also means the interface itself carries NO structure: no chain, no cause, no code. Everything 'errors can do' beyond printing is PROTOCOL — optional methods the errors package probes for:

- Unwrap() error — chain edge. fmt.Errorf %w sets it; Is/As follow it.
- Unwrap() []error — branch edge (errors.Join); the tree-walk follows these too.
- Is(error) bool — custom class matching (os.ErrNotExist matches many filesystems' not-exist via this).

The errors package's Is/As are code that type-asserts for these methods. Your custom error participates in wrapping/matching to exactly the degree it implements the optional ones — a bare Error() struct is a fully valid error that Is/As see but can't see THROUGH.

That's the layered architecture: interface for universal compatibility, protocol for capability. Adding capability never breaks compatibility — old errors without the new methods simply don't offer the new behavior, nothing breaks. When you understand error as 'one method plus optional protocol,' the whole errors package stops being magic — it's plumbing over an interface any type can join.
